title: Starch blocking crochet lace
subtitle: Using starch or sugar solution to stiffen doilies and lace motifs
excerpt: Wet blocking wool gives you drape and dimension; starch blocking gives you structure. Doilies, lace medallions, and Christmas snowflakes need to hold an open, rigid shape that water alone cannot achieve. A starch or sugar solution soaks into the fibres and sets them hard.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework, 1886, Project Gutenberg #20776. Weldon's Practical Crochet, 1880s to 1900s, Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: A finishing method that stiffens crochet lace by soaking it in a starch or sugar solution and pinning it to shape while wet, leaving it to dry rigid.
A small decorative loop formed from a short chain, used as an edging or joining point in lace crochet.

content.text: is the finishing method for crochet lace that needs to hold a rigid, open shape: doilies, snowflakes, decorative medallions, and lace collars. You soak the finished piece in a starch or sugar solution, pin it to shape on a blocking mat, and leave it to dry completely. The stiffener soaks into the fibres and holds the structure in place once dry. A wet-blocked wool shawl has drape; a starch-blocked doily sits flat and open like a plate.

items.name: Blocking mat or polystyrene board
items.note: Must be large enough to take the pinned piece flat

items.name: Rust-proof T-pins
items.note: Standard blocking pins rust and leave marks on white cotton

items.name: Stiffener solution
items.note: Commercial fabric stiffener, diluted 1:1 with water; or liquid starch from a laundry product; or a thick sugar solution (1 part sugar dissolved in 3 parts boiling water, cooled)

items.name: Bowl or tub
items.note: Large enough to submerge the piece fully

items.name: Clean towel
items.note: To remove excess moisture before pinning

items.name: Measuring tape
items.note: To verify finished dimensions against the pattern

content.text: Weave in all ends on the finished piece. Starch sets the fabric permanently; ends must be secure before you start.
Submerge the piece in the stiffener solution. Press it gently to saturate every part of the fabric. Leave it to soak for 5 minutes.
Lift the piece out and squeeze gently. Do not wring. Roll it briefly in a clean towel to remove most of the moisture. The piece should be damp, not dripping.
Lay the piece on the blocking mat. Working from the centre out, pin each chain loop and each
open with a pin. Pull each point firmly before pinning so the lace geometry is fully open.
Check measurements against the pattern. A round doily should measure the stated diameter; pin any point that is pulling in.
Leave to dry at room temperature for at least 12 hours. Do not use heat; a fan oven or hairdryer will set the stiffener unevenly. The piece must be bone-dry before the pins come out.
Remove pins. The piece should hold its shape without support.

The concentration of the stiffener controls the result. A 1:1 dilution of commercial fabric stiffener gives a firm finish that still has a little drape. Undiluted stiffener produces a rigid result that resists handling. The sugar solution falls between the two; it is also reversible: soaking in plain water dissolves the sugar and returns the fabric to its natural state, which is useful for seasonal decorations.

items.symptom: The piece dried with a yellowish or stiff-feeling sheen
items.cause: Too much stiffener was left in the fabric, or a concentrated solution was used on a fine cotton.
items.fix: Rinse in plain water to remove the excess, re-soak in a diluted solution, and re-pin. On future pieces, use a weaker solution for fine cotton thread.

items.symptom: The lace points did not hold their shape after the pins came out
items.cause: The piece was not fully dry before unpinning, or the stiffener was too dilute.
items.fix: Return the piece to the mat, re-pin, and leave for a further 6 hours. If the solution was too weak, remove the pins, re-soak in a stronger solution, and repeat.

items.symptom: Pin marks are visible in the finished piece
items.cause: Non-rust-proof pins were used and left a mark, or the pins distorted the fibres at the pinning point.
items.fix: Use T-pins or stainless steel blocking pins only. Place pins into chain loops rather than through yarn strands where possible.

content.text: A simple round doily worked in crochet cotton at a 2.5 mm hook is the standard test for starch blocking. Work a 20 cm diameter piece and block it twice, once with a dilute solution and once with a stronger one, so you can see the difference in rigidity. Once the technique feels reliable, starch-blocked snowflakes for tree decorations are a good seasonal project.
